problem_markdown: A set contains 1985 distinct positive integers, with no prime divisor greater than 26. Prove that four distinct members have product equal to an integer fourth power.
solutions_markdown:
Only the nine primes $2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23$ can occur. Assign each integer the nine-bit vector of its prime-exponent parities. There are $2^9=512$ vectors, so any 513 available integers contain a pair whose product is a square.

Choose 513 disjoint such pairs successively. This is possible: even after 512 pairs have been removed, $1985-1024=961>512$ integers remain. Write the pair products as $b_1^2,\ldots,b_{513}^2$.

Apply the same parity-vector pigeonhole argument to the 513 integers $b_i$. Two, say $b_i,b_j$, have product $c^2$. The four original integers in those two disjoint pairs then have product $b_i^2b_j^2=c^4$. Their distinctness is guaranteed by the disjoint pairing.
